name: Nankunshen Daitian Temple
address: No. 976, Kunjiang, Beimen District, Tainan City
description: Nearly every Wangye temple in Taiwan traces its roots back to one place — Nankunshen Daitian Temple in Beimen, Tainan, where branch temples return to 'pay respects to the ancestor.' It is, quite literally, the head temple of Wangye (Royal Lords) worship in Taiwan. This National Monument enshrines the Five Royal Lords — Lords Li, Chi, Wu, Zhu, and Fan — and holds a three-star rating in the Michelin Green Guide. The grounds are vast: the towering Lingxiao Treasure Hall stands on one side, the Jiangnan-style 'Da Kun Garden' on the other, every surface alive with master cut-porcelain, stone carving, and painting — no wonder it has been called a 'museum of traditional Taiwanese architecture.' When the pilgrimage season arrives on the Royal Lords' birthday, the drums and gongs of hundreds of branch temples' processions come pouring back to the mother temple — one of the most spectacular religious sights in southern Taiwan.
history: The story begins in 1661, around the time Koxinga arrived in Taiwan, making this one of the oldest Wangye temples on the island. Its most legendary chapter is the 'contest of magic' between the Five Royal Lords and the 'Child Lord' (Gina Gong) of the neighboring Wanshan Hall — the two sides fought over the same auspicious plot of land until, unable to prevail against each other, they struck a pact to share the incense offerings, and to this day both stand side by side on the site. Through repeated Qing-dynasty expansions and large-scale renovation in the Japanese era, the temple grew ever grander. Every year in the late fourth lunar month, the 'Nankunshen Grand Temple Fair' draws around a million worshippers — the largest Wangye festival in Taiwan. In 2012 it was registered as a National Monument, and its Koji pottery, wood carving, and stone work remain a must-see for lovers of traditional craft.

name: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple
address: No. 18, Ln. 227, Sec. 2, Yongfu Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple was the first official Mazu temple in Taiwan — and it hides in the lanes of the West Central District, in what was once the palace of Prince Ningjing, Zhu Shugui of the Ming. It is the only Mazu temple in Taiwan converted from a royal residence, and its stature shows. After Admiral Shi Lang took Taiwan, he turned the palace into a Tianfei (Heavenly Consort) shrine, later elevated to a Tianhou (Empress of Heaven) temple, making it the heart of Mazu worship in the Qing era — imperial plaque after imperial plaque hangs within. Those seeking love shouldn't miss the Yue Lao (Matchmaker God) in the rear hall: he is said to look after the unrequited and to warm a cooling romance, and in Tainan his efficacy is the stuff of legend.
history: In 1684, Admiral Shi Lang petitioned the Kangxi Emperor to build this temple by imperial decree — the only Mazu temple in Taiwan so commissioned, which is how it earned the name 'Grand Tianhou Temple' and the highest rank in the state sacrificial rites. The ground beneath it had been the residence of Prince Ningjing, Zhu Shugui of the Ming — a princely mansion turned Mazu temple as one dynasty gave way to the next. Its official status gave it a solemn, imposing layout, and the gold-faced Mazu statue in the main hall ranks the highest of any Mazu temple in Taiwan. Within, precious Qing imperial plaques such as 'Radiant over the Seas' survive, and it is now a National Monument. And the efficacious Yue Lao in the rear hall is, for generations of Tainan locals, the first name that comes to mind when praying for love — one of the most popular matchmaking sites in the old capital.

name: Tainan Grand Martial Temple
address: No. 229, Sec. 2, Yongfu Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: The Tainan Grand Martial Temple is the only Guan Di temple in Taiwan enrolled in the official state rites, standing shoulder to shoulder with the Grand Mazu Temple in the West Central District. What catches the eye first is its 66-meter undulating red gable wall — a sweeping, rolling expanse praised as 'the finest in Jiangnan' and a must-shoot for photographers visiting Tainan. Behind it, three halls unfold in a strict, dignified layout around the main deity, Guan Sheng Di Jun (Guan Gong), whose statue gazes out with fierce, piercing eyes. Alongside him sit Guanyin Bodhisattva and a Yue Lao (Matchmaker God) with a very particular specialty — this one severs bad romances and wards off scheming rivals, for those who need a clean, swift break from the wrong relationship.
history: In 1665, Zheng Jing — son of Koxinga — built this temple, first called the 'Grand Guan Di Temple,' the earliest official Guan Di temple in Taiwan. Its main gate faces Chihkan Tower directly, civil and martial gazing at each other across the street in the old capital's distinctive 'civil-and-martial facing' arrangement; and because it held state-ritual rank, it was paired with the Tainan Confucius Temple as the city's 'civil temple and martial temple.' Repeated Qing-dynasty renovations established today's three-hall layout, with the majestic Guan Di enthroned in the main hall. Its greatest treasure is the plaque reading 'Da Zhang Fu' (A True Man), brushed by the hand of the Yongzheng Emperor. Together with its renowned Yue Lao and the many attendant temples of the surrounding Liuhe precinct, this quarter forms one of the most complete temple clusters in old Tainan — and is today a National Monument.

name: Fo Guang Shan (Buddha's Light Mountain)
address: No. 153, Xingtian Rd., Dashu Dist., Kaohsiung City
description: From a stretch of barren hillside to more than three hundred branch temples across the globe, Fo Guang Shan (Buddha's Light Mountain) is the largest Buddhist monastery in Taiwan, set in Dashu District, Kaohsiung. One of Taiwan's four great Buddhist orders, it was founded single-handedly in 1967 by Venerable Master Hsing Yun and enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha and Amitabha Buddha. Its best-known landmark is the Buddha Memorial Center: eight pagodas line the Path to Buddhahood, drawing the eye toward the colossal Buddha statue at its end. Fo Guang Shan is famed for promoting 'Humanistic Buddhism' — the conviction that the Dharma belongs not on some remote mountaintop but woven into everyday life.
history: In 1949 Master Hsing Yun came to Taiwan with the Nationalist government; in 1967 he bought a tract of barren hillside in Dashu, Kaohsiung, and began to build — and Fo Guang Shan was born. No one could have guessed that this scrubby hill would grow, over the next fifty-odd years, into an internationally renowned center of Buddhism. In 2011 the Buddha Memorial Center was completed, and it soon became the most important religious tourism destination in southern Taiwan, drawing several million visitors a year.

name: Xingang Fengtian Temple
address: No. 53, Xinmin Rd, Xingang Township, Chiayi County
description: At Xingang Fengtian Temple in Chiayi County, the Tiger Lord (Hu Ye) doesn't crouch beneath the altar table as he does almost everywhere else — here he has been invited up onto the altar itself, and that is what makes this Mazu temple so distinctive. As the local saying goes, 'Benggang has its Herald, Xingang has its Tiger Lord,' a nod to how celebrated this temple's Tiger Lord has become. Fengtian Temple is long known as the home of the 'First Mazu of Taiwan,' its halls filled with relics and plaques bearing witness to more than three hundred years of history. Each year during the great Dajia Mazu pilgrimage, the goddess's palanquin makes a point of resting here — making the temple a place worshippers from across Taiwan journey to once a year.
history: In 1700, the monk Shubi carried a golden Mazu statue across the sea from Meizhou, the goddess's homeland, and first built a temple at Benggang — today's Beigang in Yunlin — the Benggang Tianhou Temple. Fate turned in 1799, when the Benggang (Beigang) River flooded, sweeping away the old temple and the settlement around it; the faithful carried the Mazu statue to Mayuanliao — present-day Xingang — and rebuilt, naming the new temple Fengtian. It is from this shared origin that the long-running dispute between Xingang Fengtian and Beigang Chaotian temples over the 'orthodox First Mazu of Taiwan' springs. Generations of restoration have left behind exquisite cut-porcelain and Koji pottery — the works of the Koji master Ye Wang being the temple's crowning treasure. And each year, the destination of the great Dajia Mazu pilgrimage is none other than this temple.

name: Tainan Tiantan (Altar of Heaven)
address: No. 16, Ln. 84, Sec. 2, Zhongyi Rd., West Central Dist., Tainan City
description: Tainan Tiantan — commonly called the 'Heaven Lord Temple' (Tiangong Temple) — sits in the heart of the West Central District and was the first official Altar of Heaven built in Taiwan, dedicated to the supreme Jade Emperor (Yuhuang Dadi). Step into the plain, solemn main hall and look up: there hangs a plaque bearing a single character, 'One' (一), bestowed by the Xianfeng Emperor and hailed as the most valuable plaque in all Taiwan. The meaning is wonderfully clever — Heaven is supreme, and however many principles there may be under Heaven, not one of them is greater than that single word, 'One.' On the ninth day of the first lunar month, the 'Jade Emperor's Birthday,' worshippers lay out lavish offerings of whole pigs and goats — one of the most solemn days in the old capital's calendar.
history: In 1854, the merchants and gentry of the old capital pooled their funds to raise this altar — the first official Altar of Heaven in Taiwan devoted to the Jade Emperor. Qing-dynasty officials performed the annual rites of Heaven-worship here, giving the temple the lofty standing of the state sacrificial cult. Within, several Qing imperial plaques survive, and among them the single-character 'One' plaque is the most precious of all — the temple's great treasure, and the very thing countless visitors travel here to see for themselves.

name: Tainan Confucius Temple
address: No. 2, Nanmen Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: High above the main gate hangs the plaque 'First Academy in Taiwan,' bestowed by the Kangxi Emperor — a single line that captures the standing of the Tainan Confucius Temple, the first Confucian temple in Taiwan and the highest seat of learning in the Qing era. Set in the West Central District, it follows the traditional 'school on the left, temple on the right' plan, grand and dignified. Though not a Taoist temple, it carries immense weight in Taiwan's folk belief and cultural inheritance. Each year on September 28th, Confucius's birthday, the 'Sacrificial Ceremony to Confucius' is still conducted according to ancient rites, faithfully preserving the 'Ba Yi' eight-row ceremonial dance — an essential stop for anyone drawn to Chinese culture and Confucian thought.
history: In 1665, Zheng Jing acted on the counsel of his adviser Chen Yonghua and raised this Confucius temple — the purpose plain enough: to promote learning and cultivate talent on this newly settled land. Through repeated Qing-dynasty additions and repairs, it grew to its present scale. During the Japanese colonial period the temple was for a time requisitioned for other uses, its Confucian rites restored only after the war. Today it stands as a National Monument and the center of Confucian culture in Taiwan.

name: Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia)
address: No. 212, Sec. 2, Minzhu Rd, West Central District, Tainan City
description: Chihkan Tower is not a temple but one of the most famous historic sites in the West Central District — and a symbol of Tainan itself. It began life as 'Fort Provintia,' built by the Dutch, and the Haishen (Sea God) Temple and Wenchang Pavilion seen today rise directly atop the foundations of that old Dutch fort. The garden's greatest draw is the 'Nine Stone Tortoises Bearing Steles,' bestowed by the Qianlong Emperor to commemorate the quelling of the Lin Shuangwen uprising — objects of real historical weight. Up in the Wenchang Pavilion stands Kuixing, God of Examinations, vermilion brush in hand, which is why this ancient site doubles as a place where crowds of students come to pray for success in their exams.
history: In 1653 the Dutch raised Fort Provintia here. In 1661 Koxinga took the fort and established 'Chengtian Prefecture' as the island's highest seat of government, and Chihkan changed hands. Through earthquakes and local uprisings the old ramparts largely crumbled, and it was only in the Guangxu era that the Haishen Temple, Wenchang Pavilion, and Wuzi Shrine were built one by one on the site. What visitors see today rests mostly on those rebuilt foundations — Dutch fortress and Chinese pavilion stacked one atop the other, a rare historical scene where two architectural traditions meet.

name: Donggang Donglong Temple
address: No. 21-1, Donglong St, Donggang Township, Pingtung County
description: Before you even set foot inside Donglong Temple in Donggang, Pingtung, the blazing 'Golden Archway' out front stops you in your tracks — built at a cost of over a hundred million New Taiwan dollars and dazzling in the sunlight. This celebrated Wangye temple of southern Taiwan is dedicated to Lord Wen (Wenfu Qiansui) and serves as the spiritual heart of Donggang. What truly made it famous across the nation, though, is the triennial 'Donggang Welcoming the Royal Lords Peace Festival' — the burning of the King Boat — now a designated National Important Folk Cultural Asset, a vast and mysterious event that draws tens of thousands from home and abroad each time. The temple is also known for its 'Ji Gai' ritual, a ceremonial spanking believed to turn one's luck and drive away misfortune.
history: In the Qianlong era — around the 1770s — the fishermen of Donggang pooled their money to build this temple to Lord Wen. What all Taiwan remembers it for, though, is the 'Welcoming the Royal Lords Peace Festival' held once every three years. Over eight days, the rite runs from 'Fetching the Water,' when the touring Royal Lord is welcomed ashore, to the final night's 'Sending Off the Kings,' when the magnificent King Boat is set ablaze to carry the Lord back to Heaven — every stage bound by strict ancient ceremony. The boat itself is built by local craftsmen using traditional techniques, reaching over ten meters in length, its beams carved and painted with breathtaking care. On the night of the sending-off, tens of thousands gather along the shore to watch the flames devour the vessel inch by inch — a sight both magnificent and profoundly moving. The Donggang Welcoming of the Royal Lords is today a National Important Folk Custom.

name: Chiayi City God Temple
address: No. 168, Wufeng N. Rd, East District, Chiayi City
description: Of all the county-level City God temples in Taiwan, only the City God of the Chiayi City God Temple was enfeoffed by the hand of an emperor himself — in 1875 the Guangxu Emperor conferred upon him the title 'Marquis of Suijing,' a rank of divine standing that stands alone. This old temple in Chiayi's East District keeps its incense fires burning bright; the building seen today was reconstructed in 1940, blending Minnan and Japanese-colonial architectural styles. In 2015 it was elevated to a National Monument, a witness to more than three hundred years of faith in Chiayi. Rich in Qing-dynasty plaques, stone steles, and wood carvings, it comes most alive during the seventh-lunar-month City God festival — one of the grandest religious events in the city.
history: The temple's beginnings were humble: in 1694, Zhuluo County first raised a simple City God shrine holding nothing but a spirit tablet. In the winter of 1715, the Zhuluo magistrate Zhou Zhongxuan donated his own salary to build a proper temple, which was reconstructed again in 1765. Its true moment of glory came in 1875, when the Guangxu Emperor enfeoffed the Chiayi City God as 'Marquis of Suijing' — the only county-level City God in all Taiwan to receive an imperial title. The present temple was completed in a 1940 rebuild that preserves the craftsmanship of the Japanese colonial era, and in 2015 it was designated a National Monument.

name: Fongshan Longshan Temple
address: No. 7, Zhongshan Rd, Fongshan District, Kaohsiung City
description: Fongshan Longshan Temple is the best-preserved of all the Qing-era Longshan temples surviving in Taiwan, a designated National Monument in the Fongshan District of Kaohsiung. While most Longshan temples were founded by Sanyi immigrants from Quanzhou, this one traces its incense to the Anhai Longshan Temple in Quanzhou, giving it a lineage all its own. Dedicated to Guanyin Bodhisattva, the temple is prized above all for its cut-porcelain and clay-sculpture work — masterfully executed, beautifully preserved, and the very thing that draws connoisseurs to make the trip. As the foremost of Fongshan's four ancient temples, it stands in quiet, weathered dignity, a witness to the rise and fall of the old walled city and an important resource for the study of traditional Taiwanese architecture and folk belief.
history: The temple is said to have been founded in the early Qianlong era, though the exact date is lost to record. A touching folk tale survives: an oil peddler from Fujian, passing through, hung the Guanyin incense amulet he carried on a guava tree to rest — and left without it. That night the amulet glowed in the dark like a bright pearl, and the villagers, certain the Bodhisattva had shown herself, built a temple to enshrine her. Many restorations followed, the most important in 1764, when the county magistrate Wang Yingzeng led a major rebuild. Much of what stands today reflects repairs from the Daoguang era and the Japanese colonial period.

name: Checheng Fu'an Temple
address: No. 51, Fu'an Rd, Checheng Township, Pingtung County
description: Place a sheet of gold paper at the mouth of the furnace and it is drawn in, sheet after sheet, all on its own — the 'divine cash-counting machine' furnace at Fu'an Temple in Checheng, Pingtung, whose precisely engineered convection leaves worshippers marveling. Checheng Fu'an Temple is the largest Earth God (Tudi Gong) temple in Taiwan and the spiritual center of the Hengchun Peninsula, its incense fires never dimming. The main deity, Fude Zhengshen, wears a dragon robe and an official's cap — nothing like the humble Earth God figures seen elsewhere — a sign of the exalted rank conferred on him by an emperor. Built in the grand palace style of northern China, it is the finest place to stop on the drive south toward Kenting.
history: In the Guangxu era — around the 1880s — the early settlers of Checheng pooled their funds to build this temple to Fude Zhengshen. Its grandeur set it apart from the small, modest Earth God shrines found elsewhere: legend holds that the Qing governor Liu Mingchuan, touring the south, was so struck by the temple's imposing air that he conferred upon it the name 'Fu'an Temple.' After the war it was expanded several times, its main hall rising lofty and resplendent in gold. Fu'an Temple's best-known tradition is the 'race for the first incense': in the countdown from New Year's Eve to the first day of the lunar year, worshippers surge forward to plant the very first incense stick — an electric, jostling scene. And with Kenting National Park close at hand, the temple has become a favorite waypoint for travelers heading south to pray for blessings.

name: Pingtung Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple
address: No. 174, Ren'ai St., Jiuru Township, Pingtung County
description: The Jiuru Sanshan Guowang Temple in Pingtung is one of the oldest temples to the Three Mountain Kings in Taiwan, a designated National Monument resting quietly in Jiuru Township. It enshrines the three kings of Mounts Jin, Ming, and Du, and its architecture keeps a strongly Hakka temple character — plain, restrained, and dignified. The Qing-dynasty steles and plaques within record the hardships of Hakka pioneers carving out a life on the frontier of southern Taiwan. Jiuru lies at the heart of Pingtung's Hakka settlements, and to this day the temple remains a place where local Hakka come to worship, to gather and deliberate, and to renew a shared sense of identity — a living witness to the Liudui Hakka community's opening of the Pingtung Plain.
history: Around 1700, in the Kangxi era, the earliest Hakka migrants from Guangdong raised this temple. At the time the Pingtung Plain was still a frontier where indigenous territory met Han settlement, and the Hakka pioneers carried the incense of the Three Mountain Kings from their old homeland, making the temple both a spiritual anchor and the center of their community. Repeated restorations followed, and a rebuild in the Daoguang era set down the basic layout seen today. For its long history and Hakka cultural value, it was designated a National Monument. The Liudui Hakka Cultural Park now takes this area as its core — and for anyone wanting to understand the Hakka history of southern Taiwan, this Three Mountain Kings temple is not to be missed.

name: Xinying Taizi Temple
address: No. 45-2, Taizigong, Taibei Vil., Xinying District, Tainan City
description: Nearly every Nezha temple in Taiwan can trace its incense back to this one. Xinying Taizi Temple is the head temple of Marshal of the Central Altar and the founding temple of the tradition, with branches across the island. The great days come in the ninth lunar month: around the god's birthday, palanquins from branch temples everywhere return to Xinying for incense, the roads filling with electronic-music Nezha troupes and processional performers — one of the largest religious celebrations in Taiwan. The grounds hold an old temple and a new one; the old hall, now a Tainan heritage site, is modest in scale but is where the root lies, while the new temple absorbs the tens of thousands who come each year. To see this faith in its earliest form, start in the old hall.
history: In 1663, five devotees — Xu Pei-yuan, Hong Ji-zhou, He Shi-ping, Zhou Yi-de, and Li Zhong-cheng — fled war with their families, carrying the image and palanquin of the Marshal of the Central Altar across the strait and landing at Yuejin Harbor in Tainan. They settled around Xinying, the worship took root among the villages, and in 1688 the temple was built, becoming the founding temple of Nezha worship in Taiwan. Over three centuries branch temples spread across the island, and every year on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month those branches return here for incense — one temple's birthday become a homecoming for an entire tradition. The old hall still stands and is a designated Tainan heritage site.
